Voxel Painting Cell Segmentation Work Instructions
Webknossos

Status: Release v1.2

Owner: Selden Koolman

Description

These are work instructions for how to implement Voxel Painting Cell Segmentation Protocol v1.2  using webknossos.

Release Summary

Broke up segmentation, mitochondria, and defect tasks into separate workflows to codify painter desire paths.

Workflow Summary

There are two stages:

  1. Initial painting
  2. Review & correction

Initial painting

For your assigned cutout:

  1. Complete the three separate tasks associated with your assigned volume or cutout:
  1. Cell segmentation
  2. Mitochondria segmentation
  3. Defect segmentation
  1. Work through one object at a time!
  2. Trace the segment/object to completion in the cell segmentation task.
  3. Inspect the object mesh and update the semantic label for the object.
  1. Use the semantic label as a way to track which objects you’ve inspected.
  2. Consider using Ben Silverman’s tampermonkey script to easily select the semantic class for a segment.
  1. Update any mitochondria or defects that are associated with the object.

Review & correction

For your assigned cutout:

  1. Open all three segmentation tasks in separate webknossos tabs.
  2. Work through each segmentation task separately.
  3. For each segmentation task, work through each object in the segment using the sidebar.
  4. For each object:
  1. Create the 3D mesh and inspect it for any glaring mistakes:
  1. Look for clear merge or split errors.
  2. Look for any dust.
  3. Look for cases where the same segment ID was used for two objects.
  1. Inspect the object’s semantic label and verify it. If you disagree, change the label.
  2. Scroll through the 3D image and inspect for any glaring mistakes related to the boundary of the object:
  1. Look for egregious over- or underpainting.
  2. Make sure myelin is handled properly.
  3. Look for invaginations that may have been missed.
  1. If at any point you catch an error, correct it.

In-task workflow

Webknossos settings and tools

  1. Paint (or volume) opacity

  1. Keep your paintbrush’s opacity around 60. This will make it easier to see if you are overpainting a segment’s borders.
  1. This setting is the opacity slider under “Volume” in the top-left sidebar (accessible via keyboard shortcut 🅺)

  1. Overwriting

  1. Set overwriting (overlapping circles ❍, top right) to “Only overwrite empty areas.” This prevents you from accidentally painting over previously completed segments.

  1. Brush size

  1. Don’t use brushes smaller than 7vx in diameter unless absolutely necessary: they have hard square edges that make painting rounded segments more difficult, and their small size slows you down. (Top right, ≋)

Painting step-by-step

  1. Scroll through the volume and identify the largest, simplest cell in the volume. This is what you should paint first.
  2. Zoom in on the segment: your scale bar at the bottom-right corner of your view pane should be 500 or 200nm.
  1. At this point, you have several options:
  1. If the cell is very large, paint an outline of the cell within its border, then use the paint-bucket tool to fill in your outline.
  1. Outline border:
  1. Fill by clicking inside the border you’ve just drawn with the Fill Tool (paint bucket, top right):
  1. You can also paint several small loops, allowing each one to autofill:
  1. small loop fill tracing.mp4
  1. If the cell isn’t too large, paint the outline (as in step 4a) in one stroke, without stopping, and Webknossos will automatically fill in the outline for you.
  2. If the cell is large and has distinct and clearly defined borders, use the quick-select tool (top right, ⬚)  to  draw a box around it and let Webknossos attempt to fill in the segment automatically. This may then need some cleaning up with the brush/eraser.
  1. Drawing the box over the segment:
  1. Result:
  1. Paint the interior of the segment manually, using just a brush, as a last resort. You shouldn’t be painting most segments this way.
  2. Maintain as consistent as possible a distance from the cell membrane (black border) in your painting, not only within a single slide, but for every slide on which a segment appears, and for every subsequent segment.
  1. Repeat this process for every slide on which the segment appears. (Only trace one segment at a time!) Trace the segment to completion.
  1. “To completion” means the object either (1) exits the volume at one end and terminates in-volume on the other, (2) exits the volume at both ends, or (3) connects to another object at one end and (3.1) terminates or (3.2) exits at the other.
  2. An object should not terminate in-volume at both ends. Only allow this to happen if you are unsure of any possible connection to another object or continuation.
  1. As you’re painting, scroll back and forth through the slides frequently to see if you’ve mispainted anything or mistaken a border. Flashing the alpha on and off (keyboard shortcut 3️⃣) as you scroll will also help.
  2. Once you have completed tracing the segment, mesh it.
  1. Find your segment in the segment list on the far-right sidebar (accessible with keyboard shortcut 🅻) and open the context menu (⋯). Select “Compute Mesh (ad hoc).”
  1. This will create a rough 3D mesh of your segment in the 3D view pane.
  1. If you cannot see the 3D pane, click “restore tabset” 🗗 at the top right of your 2D pane to make it visible.
  1. Inspect the mesh. First, look to make sure the segment “makes sense:” are there pieces sticking out that seem like they shouldn’t belong? Floating disconnected parts or pixels? If you spot any of these issues, fix them in your segmentation by erasing/painting first, then refresh the mesh.
  1. An ad-hoc segment mesh:
  1. Once there are no obvious issues in the mesh, use the mesh and the image to determine what kind of neurite you’ve traced. (Dendrite? Axon? Glia? etc.)
  1. Use the visual glossary here to help you make decisions.
  1. Rename the segment with the appropriate segment type label.
  2. Turn now to your mitochondria task.
  3. Find the same cell you just painted in the cell segmentation task. If it contained any mitochondria, segment only those, using the same painting methods and practices you would with an entire cell.
  4. Open your defects task. If there were any defects in the microscopy images in the cell you just annotated (cracks, folds, tears, or missing areas of data), annotate those here.
  5. Move on to the next segment in your cell segmentation task and repeat the protocol from step 3, moving on to the next largest cell in your volume.

Best practices for voxel-painting

Zoom levels

  1. Always zoom in on the segment you’re tracing so that you can see membrane details clearly when defining its borders          
  2. But also avoid working at unnecessarily high magnification! Find the sweet spot where boundaries are clear, but you can still keep an eye on your segment’s neighbours for context
  3. Adjust your zoom level dynamically throughout the tracing process, rather than staying at one level for an entire segment. This will help you “see” the segment better.

Navigation

  1. Pan regularly around your working area to inspect different parts of your segment, or to see where a segment is headed
  2. Toggle annotation opacity (alpha flashing) frequently to check your work against the underlying EM data—this is critical for catching boundary errors and for building an accurate sense of the segment in your mind’s eye!
  3. Use all these navigation tools as standard practice, not occasionally. Tracing dynamically will make you more accurate!

Brushes

  1. Select appropriate brush sizes for the task at hand and avoid extremes: 1px is too small and inefficient, 4px can give hard square edges if you’re not careful, and overly large brushes require too much cleanup. You want your brush to be able to snuggle comfortably against the inner border of your current segment, so change it often and use your judgement!
  2. Break your work into smaller enclosed shapes to leverage the autofill tool effectively. Keep individual strokes smaller rather than attempting to fill large areas in single strokes; autofill can be more efficient with multiple small enclosed regions
  3. Use the flood fill paintbucket tool when you can to improve efficiency
  4. Don’t manually fill a large segment’s interior with individual brushstrokes! Sometimes you’ll have to do this, but it shouldn’t be your go-to practice.

Borders

  • Stay completely off the dark membrane borders—never paint over them or encroach on neighboring cells! Keep a consistent amount of empty space between your paint and the inner border (anywhere from 0-3px).

Tips on using Webknossos

Updating Segment Names

In webknossos, use the left side bar (L) to pull up the “Segments” list. Click the pencil after the name for each segment and write in the label. After updating, the associated segment ID will be listed in italics to the right of the name.

Reviewing Meshes in Webknossos

At any point, you can right click on a segment or the segment name to pull up a menu of operations related to the segment. On those lists, select “Compute Mesh (ad hoc)” to compute a mesh of the segment that can be viewed in the 3D view.

If you make changes to the object, you’ll need to refresh the mesh.
